review_response_tasks.stem: Why did Lena first ask which seeds came from the prize-winning garden?
options: To prove that similar envelopes held identical seeds.
To remove every packet from the donation box.
To find evidence for a claim about their origin.
To decide which flowers would win the next prize.
review_response_tasks.rationale: 第二/三段把source问题先于表现，C来源证据正确；D未来获奖非可证目标，B全扔未做，A相似信封不证明种子同一。

review_response_tasks.stem: What was wrong with applying the note to the entire box?
options: The note had been written after the seeds were planted.
The box contained donations from more than one household.
Every packet had a different recorded date.
The delivery person had refused to carry any envelopes.
review_response_tasks.rationale: 两户packet混装而note只一donation支持B；A无先后此证，C开篇无日期，D实际已送达且未拒收。

review_response_tasks.stem: What limitation did Lena identify in the proposed planting test?
options: It could reveal only the name of the delivery person.
It would necessarily destroy every seed.
It could not establish who had supplied each packet.
It would guarantee the same flowers as in the prize-winning garden.
review_response_tasks.rationale: 第三段successful flower无household记录，C溯源不能由结果证明；B必全毁、A识deliveryperson均无据，D保证同样花正是不能推出的承诺。

review_response_tasks.stem: How did the volunteers deal with the packets not identified by photographs?
options: They assigned them equally between the two households.
They returned them to the person who won the prize.
They gave them the same origin as the three identified packets.
They recorded their source as unknown.
review_response_tasks.rationale: 第四段rest source unknown明确D；C被did not give every packet否定，B未退，A未凭均分猜来源。

review_response_tasks.stem: Which principle best describes the final display?
options: An uncertain story should be hidden if the gift is valuable.
Every donated object should be tested before anyone contacts its owner.
A successful outcome is enough to establish the history of its materials.
Known origins should be distinguished from unsupported assumptions.
review_response_tasks.rationale: 分已核三包/未知其余并列方法支持D；A隐藏不符uncertainty公开，B顺序与先联系 donors不符，C结果不证明history被第三段否定。

review_response_tasks.stem: Why was Jo dissatisfied with “Poster by Ravi”?
options: It suggested that Ravi had also made her drawing.
It announced a different date for the exhibition.
It misspelt the name of the exhibition.
It gave the secretary credit for choosing the colours.
review_response_tasks.rationale: 第二段Jo认为viewers会以为Ravi画中心图，A正确；C/B姓名日期未错，D该署名无秘书且颜色是Ravi。

review_response_tasks.stem: Who shortened the line containing both names?
options: The secretary, because the line seemed too long.
The college principal, because student names were forbidden.
Jo, because she no longer wanted to exhibit the drawing.
Ravi, because he had created every part of the poster.
review_response_tasks.rationale: 第二段secretary因space缩行支持A；C无撤展，D前句Ravi交了both names，B无校长禁名。

review_response_tasks.stem: What did Jo want when she rejected removing all names?
options: To have her name printed on every college document.
To prevent the exhibition from opening.
To show clearly what each student had contributed.
To replace Ravi as the exhibition organiser.
review_response_tasks.rationale: 第三段different contributions visible即C；A每份公文/D接任组织者/B阻展无支持且超范围。

review_response_tasks.stem: What practical limit did the club acknowledge?
options: It could not retrieve every copy already shared.
It could not replace any printed posters.
It could not change the online poster.
It could not contact either of the two creators.
review_response_tasks.rationale: 第四段could not recover every shared copy支持A；在线已改否C，可到达的印刷已换否B，前 meeting已联系否D。

review_response_tasks.stem: What was the purpose of the new planning-form question?
options: To transfer all design work to the secretary.
To guarantee that no disagreement could ever recur.
To replace descriptions of work with a single name.
review_response_tasks.rationale: 末段before publication让credit decision先讨论C；D与differentcontributions反，B明确非never保证，A非任务转交。

student_passage:
### Passage One

When volunteers at a fictional community garden opened a donated box, they found several packets of flower seeds without dates. A note on top said that the seeds came from a garden that had won a local prize. Some volunteers wanted to print the prize-winning garden's name on their own display, suggesting that the donated seeds would produce equally impressive flowers.

Lena, who kept the donation records, asked a simpler question first: which seeds had actually come from that garden? The box contained packets from two different households. Their owners had used similar paper envelopes, and the person delivering them had placed everything together. The note described one donation, not necessarily the whole box.

One volunteer proposed planting a few seeds from every packet and waiting to see what grew. Lena agreed that observing the plants might answer some questions about the seeds. It would not, however, establish who had collected them. A successful flower would carry no record of which household had supplied its packet. The group needed to separate the question of what the seeds could do from the question of where they had come from.

They contacted both donors. One still had photographs of the packets before delivery, including a small mark she had drawn on each envelope. These identified three packets. The rest could not be assigned confidently, so the garden recorded their source as unknown. It did not give every packet the identity of the best-documented ones.

The final display described the donation and the uncertainty without promising a prize-winning result. Visitors could read which packets had been identified and how. Lena considered that a more useful account than a cheerful claim that the evidence could not support. The garden could still value the gift, she explained, without presenting an attractive story about it as a fact about every seed.

### Passage Two

A student arts club at the fictional Northmere College asked Ravi to create a poster for an exhibition. He agreed to arrange the words and choose the colours. Another student, Jo, supplied a drawing that would appear in the centre. The club secretary told both that their work would be acknowledged, but no one discussed exactly how the names would be printed.

When the poster appeared, it carried the line “Poster by Ravi”. Jo felt that viewers would naturally assume he had drawn the central image as well. Ravi had not asked for that wording. He had sent a file containing both names to the secretary, who shortened it because the line seemed too long for the available space. Each person had understood the promise of acknowledgement differently.

At their meeting, Ravi suggested simply removing every name. That would avoid giving him credit for Jo's drawing, but Jo objected. Her concern was not that no one should be identified; she wanted the different contributions to be visible. The secretary then proposed a revised line: “Drawing: Jo. Layout: Ravi.” It fitted below the image after a small change to the spacing.

The club replaced the printed posters it could reach and added a correction to the online version. It could not recover every copy already shared by students. Its public note therefore identified which wording had changed instead of claiming that the mistake had disappeared everywhere. Jo accepted that practical limit, while asking the club to use the fuller description in future announcements.

The secretary later added a question to the club's planning form: how should each contribution be credited? This was not a promise that disagreements would never occur again. It made a previously hidden decision available for discussion before publication. The experience had shown that a friendly intention to acknowledge people was less precise than an agreed description of what each person had done.
